title: Bitter Lemons of Cyprus: Lawrence Durrell’s Tragedies
author: Matthew Stevenson
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-05-at-10.55.22-AM-680x515.png)

From the old fortress in Girne (in Turkish Cyprus) looking up at the Kyrenia
Mountains, in which the author Lawrence Durrell lived in the 1950s, as he
describes in his memoir Bitter Lemons of Cyprus. Photo by Matthew Stevenson.

During one of my days in Nicosia, I decided to travel north to the coastal
town of Girne, which before the division was known as Kyrenia. On my map it
was labelled as Keryneia, and some of the guide books raved about its Venetian
fortress in the old port.

I associated the town with Lawrence Durrell’s celebrated memoir, _Bitter
Lemons in Cyprus_ , which was published in 1957 and in which he writes:
“Venice will never be far from me in Cyprus – for the lion of Saint Mark still
rides the humid airs of Famagusta, of Kyrenia.”

I first read _Bitter Lemons_ in the late 1970s, around the time I read his
_Alexandria Quartet_ and some of his other books set in the Greek islands (he
lived for many years on Corfu, north of the main town). I read Durrell while
commuting to work in Manhattan, perhaps to remind myself that one reward of a
day job might be the occasional trip to the Mediterranean.

+++

In Nicosia I still had my rented bicycle, and for a while I thought that to
get to the north coast (it’s not along the Green Line) I would ride over the
Kyrenia Mountains. But the more I studied the maps (admittedly some pre-dated
partition), the more it became clear that I would once again be riding on the
shoulder of an autoroute, and by that point I had had my fill of truck
exhaust.

In the end I locked my bicycle near the mini-van station in north Nicosia, and
there paid a driver a few euros, even though the official currency for the
Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus is the Turkish lira. (I never did get to
an automated teller machine to have some lira in my pocket, but no one
minded.)

In the careening mini-van, I was glad that I had left my bicycle behind, as
the driver drove at chicken-scattering speeds and used the shoulder/bike lane
to cut around slow-moving farm equipment.

As I didn’t exactly know where I was going, I stayed on the bus until the last
stop, which was just above the historic harbor. From the bus stop, it was easy
to explore the Venetian ramparts overlooking the sea, which was angry with
February whitecaps.

I even found near the port the old Anglican Church of St. Andrew, which had a
sign out front that read: “ALL WELCOME… Baptisms By Appointment…. Funerals By
Arrangement.”

+++

Sitting in old Kyrenia made me want to reread _Bitter Lemons_ , but I didn’t
find a copy either in Girne or later back in Nicosia. Only when I got home was
I able to order one in the mail.

Durrell was in his forties when he moved to Cyprus, no doubt looking for a
cheap place in the sun to write his books and drink the local wines. He had
lived in Alexandria, Egypt, during World War II, when he was a press officer
attached to the British legation, but it was only after he left Cyprus in 1956
that the four novels of the _Quartet_ — _Justine_ , _Balthazar_ , _Mountolive_
, and _Clea_ —were published.

In effect, the four novels are one: each tells the story of various failed
love affairs from another perspective. The novels capture dissolute expatriate
lives on the edge of World War II in Egypt (Rommel’s tanks were only stopped
at el-Alamein, which is about sixty miles west of Alexandria).

I only struggled with the novels when Durrell’s language became rococo, as
when he writes about Justine:

There are some characters in this world who are marked down for self-
destruction, and to these no amount of rational argument can appeal. For my
part Justine always reminded me of a somnambulist discovered treading the
perilous leads of a high tower; any attempt to wake her with a shout might
lead to disaster. One could only follow her silently in the hope of guiding
her gradually away from the great shadowy drops which loomed up on every side.

With time and perhaps the sea at your feet, _The Alexandria Quartet_ can be a
rewarding read (and at the very least might impress your hosts in the
Hamptons).

+++

As my arrival in Girne coincided with a spring downpour, I ate lunch in a
restaurant with a glass front overlooking the Venetian walls and the sea. It
reminded me, in some ways, of Alexandria, where I went with my family in 2007.

Although we landed in Cairo on a flight from Rome, the trip began in
Alexandria, where we went in search of the Pharos lighthouse (an ancient
wonder of the world) that fell into the sea in 1303 during an earthquake.

Then, on our way to the new Alexandria library (to replace that which burned
in Roman times), we walked past Villa Ambron, where Durrell had lived on the
upper floor from 1943-45.

Except for a few buildings scattered around the city, most of colonial
Alexandria was gone, except Durrell’s faded villa was still standing as the
city debated whether it should be restored and turned into a museum about
local history.

When we walked past it, the concrete pillars were crumbling, and there were
shutters on the windows and boards over the entrances. A woman we asked at the
library said that even though the building had been sold to a developer, there
was a good chance that Villa Ambron might be saved, due to local conservation
laws. But in Egypt (where a red light is “a suggestion”) laws are made to be
broken, and the wrecking ball took down Durrell’s writing tower in 2017 to
make way for a block of modern flats.

No wonder in the _Quartet_ Durrell spoke of “the indifference of the natural
world to the constructions of art.”

+++

What makes _Bitter Lemons_ a great book is that—as was said of F. Scott
Fitzgerald’s _This Side of Paradise_ —“it never fails to live.”

From his 1953 arrival by boat in Limassol in February until his escape from
the growing civil unrest in 1956, Durrell tells the stories of his island
life—his endless coffees with neighbors, his romantic infatuations besides
many beaches, his days as a school teacher in the mountains, and his last act
as a government official reporting to the governor in a time of growing
conflict.

Best of all, he tells his stories as if writing a long letter to a friend:

> But I had already begun to see the island as whole, building my picture of
> it from the conversations of my host. With him I spent three winters snowed
> up on Troodos, teaching in a village school so cold that the children’s
> teeth chattered as they wrote; with him I panted and sweated in the
> ferocious August heat of the plains; suffered from malaria at Larnaca; spent
> holidays among the rolling vineyards of Paphos in search of vines to
> transplant; like him I came back always to the Kyrenia range, to cool my
> mind and gladden my heart with its greenness, its carpets of wild anemones,
> its castles and monasteries. It was like returning to a fertile island from
> a barren one – from Cephalonia to Corfu.

The last part of the book—as Cyprus is subject to increasing political
violence, most at the hands of Greeks demanding union (_enosis_ is the term
often used) with Greece—is largely about the house he buys and restores in the
hillside village of Bellapaix (later Bellapais), at least when he’s not
drinking coffee under what he calls the “Tree of Idleness.”

The sprawling row house (wedged into a steep hillside) had a series of
connected rooms and arched hallways, and sitting well above Kyrenia the
elegant garden caught cooling breezes even during the worst of the summer
heat. It was a short drive down to the sea. He writes nostalgically:

The dawn was breaking before we were ready almost, rushing out of the night-
sea beyond Cape Andreas, a steeply mounting flush upon the bronze faces of the
mountains. A dense dew lay upon everything as we drove back through the silent
fields to Kyrenia for breakfast. There were to be many such mornings, many
such evenings spent in good fellowship and wine, before the vagaries of
fortune and the demons of ill luck dragged Cyprus into the stock-market of
world affairs and destroyed not only the fortuitous happiness of these
friendships but, more tragically and just as surely, the old tried
relationships on which the life of the little village itself was founded.

+++

The political violence that drove Durrell away from his job at Government
House and off the island was an early round of the troubles that ended in 1974
with Cyprus in partition.

In the mid-1950s, followers of Archbishop Makarios III sought to drive the
Turks off the island and to unite Cyprus with Greece. As well, they wanted
Cyprus’s independence from Britain. But under either scenario, colonial
officials like Durrell (despite his deep roots in Cypriot village life and
ability to speak the language) looked a lot like a target. He writes:

From the vantage-point of Whitehall, too, the angle of vision changed, for
here in London Cyprus was not only Cyprus; it was part of a fragile chain of
telecommunication centres and ports, the skeletal backbone of an Empire
striving to resist the encroachments of time. If Cyprus were to be frivolously
wished away then what of Hong Kong, Malta, Gibraltar, the Falklands, Aden –
all troubled but stable islands in the great pattern? Palestine and Suez had
been questions of foreign sovereignty; they had never been Crown possessions.
Cyprus belonged, from the point of view of geography and politics, to the
Empire’s very backbone. Must it not, then, be held at all costs?

Unfortunately for all concerned, Archbishop Makarios saw himself as a clerical
Marshal Tito, someone in the Levant who could be a bridge not just between
Greek Cypriots and Greece, but also a sympathetic ear to Eastern Europe and
Russia, who (he may have speculated) might facilitate independence from
Britain or later from NATO.

All that Cold War posing accomplished was to turn American mandarins (from the
1960s onward) into advocates for partition so that the West would not lose its
Cyprus listening posts and airfields so close to Middle Eastern oil. Even
after independence, Britain had retained what were called Sovereign Base
Areas.

Keep in mind that Durrell left Cyprus in 1956 just before Britain and France
made a colonial mess of the Suez Crisis. It was bad enough that Gamal Abdel
Nasser had the canal; as a follow-on, no one wanted to find Cyprus among the
rebellious ranks of the non-aligned.

+++

Well into _Bitter Lemons_ Durrell makes mention that he had given over a room
in his Bellapaix house to his young daughter, then about age four.

When I first heard mention of a daughter, I wondered if I had missed something
in an earlier chapter. When I went back in the book, I saw no earlier
reference to Sappho, whose mother was Eve Cohen (the inspiration for Durrell’s
Alexandrine character Justine and Durrell’s second wife). But Eve wasn’t in
his life at this time, apparently.

Durrell is one of those writers who makes little reference either to spouses
or romantic partners, except elliptically, and in _Bitter Lemons_ his mother
gets more mentions than his lovers. So it intrigued me that Durrell had a
young daughter and that she occasionally came out to Cyprus to stay with her
father.

In looking for more details about Sappho, I discovered that she had died by
suicide in 1985, at age 33, and that in letters and journals she accused her
father of raping her in 1967, when she was fourteen. Numerous obituaries of
Sappho’s short and troubled life make reference to her father’s alleged abuse,
and link it to her suicide.

I realize that authors can adopt any persona that they choose (and few cast
themselves as a child abuser), and the Durrell of _Bitter Lemons_ is humane,
engaged, good company, and eloquent with his prose. He writes as he is leaving
the island:

The white wine tasted sharp and good and as he raised his glass Panos gave me
the toast of the day: ‘That we may pass beyond’ (i.e. the present troubles)
‘and that we might emerge once more in the forgotten Cyprus – as if through a
looking-glass.’ In a way, too, he was toasting a dying affection which might
never be revived – one of those bright dreams of deathless friendship which
schoolboys still believed in, of an England and Greece which were bondsmen in
the spirit.

So spoke the Englishman who became the beacon for so many Britons who went
abroad in the 1950s and 60s, especially to the Mediterranean, in search of a
best-selling book, if not winter sun and affordable wines.

At the same time, I now find the evidence of his sexual abuse to be
overwhelming, such that I ask myself how I missed this dark side in so many of
his books. Surely it must be there, as in the _Quartet_ he writes: “Art like
life is an open secret.” And with Durrell, Daddy’s little secret most likely
claimed his daughter’s happiness and her life. And life has no more bitter
lesson.

_This is the seventh in an occasional series about travels through the Balkans
to and from the Green Line in Cyprus._
